terms.definition: Yogic breath regulation. Prāṇa is the vital breath, āyāma its extension or restraint. The classic practices come from Haṭha yoga texts.
The long cranial nerve carrying calming, 'rest and digest' signals between brain, heart, lungs and gut. Slow exhales are thought to nudge it toward calm.
Heart rate variability: the natural beat-to-beat variation in heart rhythm. Higher resting HRV usually goes with better recovery and a calmer nervous system.
Seated meditation in Zen: upright, alert, eyes lowered. Sōtō emphasises just sitting; Rinzai pairs it with kōan study.
Pāli for loving-kindness: a warm, unconditional wish for well-being, cultivated toward oneself and outward to all beings.
Remembrance of God in Sufi practice: repeating sacred names or phrases, often in rhythm with the breath.
Eastern Christian contemplative tradition of inner stillness (hesychia), known for the Jesus Prayer paired with the breath.
In Chinese thought, the vital energy or breath that moves through the body; cultivated in qigong, tai chi and Daoist meditation.
'Elixir field': energy centres in Daoist practice. The lower dantian sits a few finger-widths below the navel and is a common resting place for attention.
Breath retention in prāṇāyāma, after the inhale (antara) or the exhale (bāhya).
Breathing at around five to six breaths a minute, where heart rhythm and breath fall into step. Also called resonance breathing.
How comfortable the body is with a rising carbon-dioxide level. Gentle holds and slow exhales can raise it, which tends to ease the urge to over-breathe.
The branch of the autonomic nervous system that slows the heart and settles the body. Long exhales lean this way.
The 'fight or flight' branch of the nervous system: faster heart, sharper alertness. Useful in bursts, tiring when it stays on.
A reflex that steadies blood pressure by adjusting heart rate. Slow breathing is thought to strengthen it, part of why resonance breathing feels calming.
A gas made in the nasal passages that helps open airways and blood vessels. Humming greatly increases its release.
Breathing that lets the belly rise on the inhale, using the diaphragm rather than lifting the shoulders.
Alternate-nostril breathing; literally 'channel cleansing'. Thumb and ring finger close one nostril at a time.
'Victorious' breath: a soft ocean sound made by slightly narrowing the throat on each breath.
'Bee' breath: a long hum on the exhale, often with ears gently covered.
A hand or body gesture used in meditation, such as the cosmic mudrā of zazen (hands cupped, thumbs lightly touching).
A word or phrase repeated silently or aloud to steady attention — Buddho, So Hum, a sacred name.
'Repetition without repeating': letting a mantra such as So Hum ride on the natural breath rather than being spoken.
Mindfulness of breathing, the Buddha's sixteen-step instruction in the Ānāpānasati Sutta.
Insight meditation: clear, moment-to-moment observation of sensations and the mind, as taught in the Theravāda tradition.
Calm abiding: steadying the mind on one object (often the breath) until it settles. Also spelled shamatha.
Tibetan 'giving and taking': breathing in another's difficulty, breathing out relief. A practice of compassion.
A Zen question or story that cannot be solved by ordinary reasoning, used in Rinzai training to exhaust the thinking mind.
Walking meditation in Zen, slow and in step with the breath, done between periods of sitting.
'Yogic sleep': a guided rest lying down, moving attention through the body while staying awake at the edge of sleep.
Steady gazing at a single point, often a candle flame, to gather attention; one of the Haṭha yoga cleansing practices.
A Christian silent prayer method: return gently to a chosen sacred word whenever thoughts arise.
'Divine reading': a slow, prayerful way of reading a short text — read, reflect, respond, rest.
A Daoist practice of guiding attention (and qi) in a loop up the spine and down the front of the body.
'Standing like a post': a still standing posture from Chinese internal arts, building quiet strength and settled attention.
Forest bathing: unhurried time among trees, taking in the forest through the senses. Term coined in Japan in 1982.
Two inhales through the nose (the second a small top-up) followed by a long exhale; a fast way to offload CO₂ and settle.
Equal inhale, hold, exhale, hold — classically four counts each. Simple, steadying, widely used for composure under pressure.
Inhale four, hold seven, exhale eight: a slow pattern popularised by Dr Andrew Weil, often used before sleep.
Sensing the body's inner state — heartbeat, breath, warmth, tension. Many practices train it by returning attention inward.
Brain regions active during mind-wandering and self-referential thought. Focused attention practices tend to quiet it.
A 15th-century yoga manual by Svātmārāma describing postures, prāṇāyāma and cleansing practices.
The earliest complete collection of Buddhist scriptures, preserved in the Pāli language by the Theravāda school.
'Eight Pieces of Brocade': a classical qigong set of eight gentle movements, often done as a morning routine.
